reply_text:
Fix and tests are done and pass; now writing the test receipt, committing, reloading the serving process, and checking what the existing feedback store already holds.㊥ ("let's go with this fix now") The fix is committed and loaded in the serving process (futon2 `a3ae4c664`). A click that does grounded work but reaches or progresses none of its selected wants now records each pattern as `:no-want-effect` with no reinforcement, so the habit factor is unchanged by it. I have not run a click: I did not read your message as granting one.

㊢ (what changed) In `cascade_feedback.clj`:
- **Positive record:** now needs at least one selected want classed reached or progressed. With that, the records are the same as before.
- **No want moved:** each pattern gets the new neutral status. It is counted separately so it can be inspected, and the habit factor does not read that count.
- **Scope:** the condition is per run, not per pattern. If one want is reached, all four patterns of the cascade still get credit.

㊬ (tests) Two new tests use the selected action of the last click (four wants, four patterns) and build the want accounting with the real functions.
- **All four wants false, as that click measured:** four neutral records, factor 1.0.
- **One want true:** one "successful", three "supporting", factor above 1.
- **Old rule put back temporarily:** the first test fails on 8 assertions, so it does catch the earlier behaviour.
- **Run:** 14 tests, 87 assertions, 0 failures; lint and paren checks clean; receipt committed beside the test.

㊢ ("flag it as something that we want to investigate") I saved this as a standing note. On each of the next clicks I will show you, from the run record:
1. the selected wants;
2. which pattern produces which want;
3. each want's measurement and class;
4. the feedback record per pattern;
5. the pattern counts and habit factor before and after.

㊩ (two things the examples will run into)
- **A failed want changes nothing the next selection reads.** The per-pattern trial records are written, but marked "held" and "record-only", and they update no parameter. Only the enactment count on the habit moves.
- **The existing feedback file predates want accounting.** `data/wm-pattern-feedback/events.edn` holds 7 events from 1–4 October, 5 of them with positive credit, and the next selection still reads them. By your ruling that the earlier implementation is not evidence, they should probably not feed the rebuilt machine. I have left the file alone.

🈸 ("in the next click or two") Two decisions:
1. May codex-10 run one click now? If so, I will have it stopped after selection and after the feedback record so you can look at the values above.
2. Should the click start from an empty pattern-feedback file? I recommend yes, with the old file moved aside and kept, so the before-and-after counts in the example come only from this run.

- A click run now would end with the old census, which reports on evidence nothing writes.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-2
previous_reply_acts.text:
("keep track of how much") The run record already carries what a cost row needs. I read the producer:
- **Tokens:** `:registered-run/model-usage` lists every job the click dispatched, with its role, phase and input, output and cached counts. It also says whether the accounting is complete, partial or missing.
- **Time:** `:registered-run/timing` has per-phase times, with selection broken into sub-phases since yesterday's commits.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-2
previous_reply_acts.text:
("part of R20 as an additional criterion") A ninth row, cost.
- **Prints:** tokens and time before selection, at selection and after it, and which side the click spent most on.
- **Agrees when:** the accounting is complete, meaning every dispatched job has a usage record and the parts add up to the total.
- **No threshold yet:** I would not set a pass mark for "too many tokens". There is no basis for one until several clicks have been measured, so I can't say whether a million is a lot.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-2
previous_reply_acts.text: (what the theory offers for efficiency) Parr et al. (§10.8) treat this as bounded rationality: an agent "has to balance the costs, effort, and timeliness of computation", and "what is costly during deliberation is decreasing the entropy ... of one's beliefs before a choice". That suggests comparing what deliberation spent with how much it sharpened the choice among policies. A figure such as "nats gained per million tokens" would be my construction from that passage, not something the book defines. I would report it alongside the raw numbers first and only later consider it as a criterion.
